title: Spanish foundations
description: Four A1 Spanish lessons: first words, introductions, polite café requests, and numbers for everyday quantities. Native-speaker editorial review remains open.

units.title: Getting around
units.objective: Understand prices and quantities in everyday errands.

units.title: Finding your way
units.objective: Ask where things are and follow spoken directions.

units.title: Everyday life
units.objective: Talk about days, times, and the people around you.

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Spanish grew from Latin in Iberia, and thousands of everyday words came into both Spanish and English from Latin — nación, información, restaurante, café. You can already recognize them before you speak a word of Spanish. The words below are the first ones to say out loud: hola opens almost every conversation, gracias answers kindness, sí and no steer it.
concepts.commonError: Say hola the moment you arrive. Save adiós for leaving.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: Me llamo introduces your name: Me llamo Ana. Soy means I am and can also introduce you: Soy Ana. To ask a peer their name, use ¿Cómo te llamas? Learn this as a complete question. Mucho gusto is a useful reply when meeting someone. Spanish marks a question at both ends: ¿ ... ?.
concepts.commonError: Use me llamo for your own name and te llamas in the informal question. Do not swap me and te.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: Quisiera means I would like and makes a polite request. Learn it as a ready-to-use phrase: Quisiera un café, por favor. Both café and té take un here. Change only the drink to request tea. A shorter Un café, por favor is also useful; gracias closes the exchange.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Keep un with café and té in these requests. Remember the accents in café and té.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: Spanish numbers are useful as chunks before you calculate with them. Learn one through ten in two short runs, then use cuánto cuesta to ask a price. One coffee costs one euro; two coffees cost two euros. Un changes to una before a feminine noun such as manzana.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use cuánto for the price of one item. Keep una with manzana because it is feminine.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: Dónde means where, and it carries a written accent because it is asking a question: ¿Dónde está la estación? Directions come as short chunks worth learning whole: todo recto (straight ahead), a la izquierda (to the left), a la derecha (to the right). Spanish puts the first step first and then the next one after luego. Starting with Perdone turns a bare question into a polite one, the way excuse me does in English.

examples.target: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

concepts.commonError: Dónde asks where. Quién asks who and qué asks what. The accent on dónde marks the question and drops in the middle of a sentence.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: Cuánto cuesta asks how much something costs, and it is the standard price question. Answer with a number and euros. Caro means expensive and barato means inexpensive. To disagree, put no before the verb: No es caro. The bill is la cuenta, a feminine noun, and por favor turns it into a request.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Spanish puts no before the verb, never after it. Cost is cuesta for one thing and cuestan for several.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: Hoy means today and mañana means tomorrow. Weekdays are masculine and take el in front when you mean on that day: el lunes, on Monday. Spanish does not need a word for on here; the article does that work. Notice that mañana also means morning, and only the article and context separate them.
concepts.commonError: Mañana is both tomorrow and morning. La mañana is the morning; mañana alone in a schedule usually means tomorrow.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine, and the article changes with them: el hermano (brother), la hermana (sister), los padres (parents). The verb tener is irregular in the I form: tengo, I have. Possessives agree with the thing owned rather than the owner, so mi familia is my family and mis padres is my parents.
concepts.commonError: Tengo, not tene. Tener is irregular in the I form and it is the form you use most when talking about family.

Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.objective: Recognize and say your first Spanish words — greetings and Latin-shared words — before building any sentences.
lessons.explanation: You already know hundreds of Spanish words: nación, información, restaurante. They came into English and Spanish from Latin, the common root of Spanish, French, Italian and Portuguese — which is why the Romance languages resemble each other. Today you only say a few out loud: hola, gracias, sí, no. No sentences yet — those come next.
lessons.culturalNote: Hola works everywhere, all day. Gracias answers everything from gifts to directions.

exercises.prompt: You already know this word — friends say it a dozen times a day in Spain. «Hola» — what does it mean?
exercises.explanation: Hola. is hello — the first word to say out loud. The rest of this lesson stays this small.

exercises.prompt: Think: you meet a friend in Madrid. One word greets them before anything else. Say it in your head — then write it.
exercises.explanation: Hola. One word, said first, opens the conversation.

exercises.prompt: Nación, información, restaurante — spelled almost the same in English and Spanish. Why do you already recognize them?
answers: Spanish and English share thousands of words from Latin.
options: Spanish and English share thousands of words from Latin.
Spanish borrowed its everyday words from modern English.
exercises.explanation: Both languages inherited these words from Latin — the common root of the Romance languages. Recognition comes before production.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: Gracias.
exercises.explanation: Gracias is thank you — the second word to say out loud.

exercises.prompt: Complete the first word you say to a friend: ___
exercises.explanation: Hola. — said before everything else.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange. How many times do you read the word for thank you?
exercises.passage: — Hola ! — Hola. — Gracias ? — Sí, gracias. — No, gracias.
exercises.explanation: Every word on this page is one you already learned.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the model: first words.
exercises.explanation: Two words you can say. Replay slowly, then at normal speed.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself, ask a name, and respond to an introduction.
lessons.explanation: Me llamo introduces your name: Me llamo Ana. Soy means I am and can also introduce you: Soy Ana. To ask a peer their name, use ¿Cómo te llamas? Learn this as a complete question. Mucho gusto is a useful reply when meeting someone. Spanish marks a question at both ends: ¿ ... ?.
lessons.culturalNote: The name question uses informal te for a peer. In a more formal situation, Spanish also has an usted form; this lesson stays with the informal question.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase asks another person their name in Spanish?
exercises.explanation: Use the complete name question when meeting someone.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to introduce Ana by name.
exercises.explanation: Use me llamo for your own name and te llamas in the informal question. Do not swap me and te.

exercises.prompt: Read the first meeting. Who gives their own name?
exercises.explanation: The person who uses the name phrase introduces themself.
exercises.passage:
Ana: Hola. Me llamo Ana.
Leo: Hola. Mucho gusto.
exercises.translation:
Ana: Hello. My name is Ana.
Leo: Hello. Nice to meet you.

exercises.prompt: Say “Nice to meet you” using the short expression taught here.
exercises.explanation: Use this short response after an introduction.

exercises.prompt: Imagine meeting a new classmate. Introduce yourself as Ana, using the phrase that means “My name is”.
exercises.explanation: Use me llamo for your own name and te llamas in the informal question. Do not swap me and te.

exercises.prompt: Ask a peer “What is your name?” using the complete question taught here.
exercises.explanation: This is the name question from the lesson; recall it as a whole.

lessons.title: At the café
lessons.objective: Choose a drink and make a polite café request from memory.
lessons.explanation: Quisiera means I would like and makes a polite request. Learn it as a ready-to-use phrase: Quisiera un café, por favor. Both café and té take un here. Change only the drink to request tea. A shorter Un café, por favor is also useful; gracias closes the exchange.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

lessons.culturalNote: A greeting before a request and thanks afterward make this small exchange courteous.

exercises.prompt: You want tea. Which complete request matches your intention?
exercises.explanation: Change the drink while keeping the polite request frame.

exercises.prompt: Build the full polite request for one coffee.
exercises.explanation: Keep un with café and té in these requests. Remember the accents in café and té.

exercises.prompt: Read the café exchange. Which drink does the customer request?
exercises.explanation: The customer requests tea; the thanks closes the exchange.
exercises.passage:
Customer: Hola. Un té, por favor.
Server: Un té?
Customer: Sí. Gracias.
exercises.translation:
Customer: Hello. A tea, please.
Server: A tea?
Customer: Yes. Thank you.

exercises.prompt: Say “I would like a tea, please” using the full request frame.
exercises.explanation: Keep un with café and té in these requests. Remember the accents in café and té.

exercises.prompt: You arrive at a café and want coffee. Make the short request “A coffee, please”.
exercises.explanation: The short request still includes please.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning of this complete request: Quisiera un café, por favor.
answers: I would like a coffee, please.
exercises.explanation: This is a polite request, not a statement about having coffee.

lessons.title: Numbers and quantities
lessons.objective: Recognize one to ten, ask a price, and order a small quantity.
lessons.explanation: Count one through ten as two short runs. Then use cuánto cuesta for the price of one thing. You already have por favor from the café; attach it to a quantity to make a small, polite order.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

lessons.culturalNote: Prices may be said quickly. First listen for the number, then the item and the total.

exercises.prompt: Which Spanish number means three?
exercises.explanation: Tres is three.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to ask the price of one coffee.
exercises.explanation: Cuánto cuesta asks what one thing costs.

exercises.prompt: Say in Spanish: Two apples, please.
exercises.explanation: Dos stays the same before the plural noun manzanas.

exercises.prompt: Read the price sign. How many euros is the tea?
exercises.passage: Café: dos euros. Té: tres euros.
exercises.translation: Coffee: two euros. Tea: three euros.
exercises.explanation: Té costs tres euros on this sign.

exercises.prompt: Think: a vendor has one apple. Ask its price, then write the question.
exercises.explanation: One apple is feminine: una manzana. The price question stays cuánto cuesta.

lessons.title: Asking the way
lessons.objective: Ask where something is and follow a two-step direction.
lessons.explanation: Dónde means where, and it carries a written accent because it is asking a question: ¿Dónde está la estación? Directions come as short chunks worth learning whole: todo recto (straight ahead), a la izquierda (to the left), a la derecha (to the right). Spanish puts the first step first and then the next one after luego. Starting with Perdone turns a bare question into a polite one, the way excuse me does in English.

examples.target: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

lessons.culturalNote: In Spain you open a request to a stranger with Perdone, and you thank them even for one sentence of directions.

exercises.prompt: You need to ask where something is. Which word does that?
exercises.explanation: Dónde asks about a place. Quién asks who, and qué asks what.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange. Which direction comes first?
exercises.explanation: The first instruction is todo recto; a la izquierda comes after luego, as the second step.
exercises.passage:
Turista: Perdone, ¿dónde está la estación?
Transeúnte: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
Turista: ¡Gracias!
exercises.translation:
Tourist: Excuse me, where is the station?
Passer-by: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Tourist: Thank you!

exercises.prompt: Build the question that asks where the station is.
exercises.explanation: The opening question mark goes at the front in Spanish, and estación is feminine, so the article is la.

exercises.prompt: Ask where the bathroom is.
exercises.explanation: Baño is masculine, so the article is el.

exercises.prompt: Complete the directions: Todo recto, luego a la ___
exercises.explanation: Izquierda is left. Derecha would send the learner the other way.

exercises.prompt: Make the question polite by putting Perdone in front: ¿Dónde está la estación?
exercises.explanation: Perdone leads the sentence, and the accent on dónde drops when it is no longer opening the question.

lessons.title: Prices and paying
lessons.objective: Ask what something costs, react to the price, and ask for the bill.
lessons.explanation: Cuánto cuesta asks how much something costs, and it is the standard price question. Answer with a number and euros. Caro means expensive and barato means inexpensive. To disagree, put no before the verb: No es caro. The bill is la cuenta, a feminine noun, and por favor turns it into a request.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

lessons.culturalNote: In many Spanish bars the bill comes when you ask for it, so la cuenta, por favor is the normal way to end a meal.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks the price of something?
exercises.explanation: Cuánto asks how much and cuesta comes from costar, to cost.

exercises.prompt: Say that it is not expensive: Es caro.
exercises.explanation: No goes before the verb in Spanish.

exercises.prompt: You want to know what a coffee costs. Ask the question.
exercises.explanation: Cuesta is singular because one coffee is being priced.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that says this is very expensive.
exercises.explanation: Muy means very and it sits directly before the adjective.

exercises.prompt: Ask for the bill.
exercises.explanation: Cuenta is feminine, so the article is la.

exercises.prompt: Complete the price question: ¿___ cuesta el café?
exercises.explanation: Cuánto cuesta is the fixed frame for asking a price.

lessons.title: Days and times
lessons.objective: Name days, place an action on a day, and say what today is.
lessons.explanation: Hoy means today and mañana means tomorrow. Weekdays are masculine and take el in front when you mean on that day: el lunes, on Monday. Spanish does not need a word for on here; the article does that work. Notice that mañana also means morning, and only the article and context separate them.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish weekdays are not capitalised, which is why lunes looks the same mid-sentence as at the start of one.

exercises.prompt: Which word means today?
exercises.explanation: Hoy is today. Mañana is tomorrow, and lunes is Monday.

exercises.prompt: Read the week. What day is it today?
exercises.explanation: Hoy es miércoles gives the answer directly in the third sentence.
exercises.passage: El lunes trabajo. El martes aprendo español. Hoy es miércoles. Mañana es jueves.
exercises.translation: On Monday I work. On Tuesday I learn Spanish. Today is Wednesday. Tomorrow is Thursday.

exercises.prompt: According to the week you just read, which day comes next?
exercises.explanation: Mañana es jueves names the following day.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that says today is Wednesday.
exercises.explanation: Hoy first, then es, then the day.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: Mañana ___ jueves.
exercises.explanation: The same frame as Hoy es miércoles, with mañana in place of hoy.

exercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Monday.
exercises.explanation: Hoy es plus the day name, the same frame as the model.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: El lunes trabajo.
exercises.explanation: Spanish marks on with the article el rather than a separate word.

lessons.title: Family and people
lessons.objective: Name close family members and say who you have, with the right article.
lessons.explanation: Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine, and the article changes with them: el hermano (brother), la hermana (sister), los padres (parents). The verb tener is irregular in the I form: tengo, I have. Possessives agree with the thing owned rather than the owner, so mi familia is my family and mis padres is my parents.
lessons.culturalNote: Familia in Spanish often stretches to grandparents, aunts and cousins, not just the household.

exercises.prompt: Which one means the sister?
exercises.explanation: Hermana is the sister. Hermano is the brother, and padres are the parents.

exercises.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother.
exercises.explanation: Tener is irregular, so the I form is tengo rather than tene.

exercises.prompt: Which one is correct for I have a sister?
exercises.explanation: Hermana is feminine, so the article is una.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that says this is my family.
exercises.explanation: Familia is feminine, so the demonstrative is esta and the possessive is mi.

exercises.prompt: Change one sister into two sisters: Tengo una hermana.
exercises.explanation: The plural adds -s to hermana, and una becomes dos.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: Mis ___ viven en Madrid.
exercises.explanation: Padres is plural, which is why the verb is viven rather than vive.

exercises.prompt: Read about the family. Where do the parents live?
exercises.explanation: The last sentence places the parents in Madrid.
exercises.passage: Mi familia es pequeña. Mi hermano se llama Max. Mi hermana se llama Ana. Mis padres viven en Madrid.
exercises.translation: My family is small. My brother is called Max. My sister is called Ana. My parents live in Madrid.
